name: Burg Wiesberg
kurzbeschreibung: Burg Wiesberg in Tobadill: Defiant 13th-century hilltop castle, perched spectacularly above the Trisanna gorge and the 87-metre-high Arlberg railway viaduct.
beschreibung:
Overview

The imposing Burg Wiesberg (also known as Schloss Wiesberg) perches on a daring rock spur at roughly 1,050 metres above sea level on the border between the municipalities of Tobadill and Pians in the Tiroler Oberland. Situated at the junction of the Stanzertal and the entrance to the Paznaun valley, this high-medieval fortification commands the deeply carved, wild Trisanna gorge. The ensemble is world-renowned for the dramatic contrast between historic defensive architecture and audacious railway civil engineering: directly alongside the battlements of the castle, the heritage-listed, 87-metre-high Trisannabrücke of the Arlbergbahn spans the roaring mountain waters of the Trisanna.

History & Civil Engineering

The origins of the spur castle date back to the 13th century: it was presumably erected by ministerial retainers of the Bistum Chur and the Counts of Montfort to control militarily the strategic bridge across the Trisanna and the packhorse trail leading into Paznaun. The stronghold is first documented in 1271 with Hugo von Wiesberg and in 1288 in the comprehensive land registry of Graf Meinhard II. von Tirol. Following the bloody Rottenburger Fehde in 1411, the castle fell to the Tyrolean sovereigns and henceforth served as a sovereign administrative seat. From the 16th century, the Habsburgs granted the castle as a fief to the Counts of Wolkenstein-Rodenegg. During the Tyrolean uprising in November 1809, Wiesberg achieved historic fame when local sharpshooters from Paznaun and the Stanzertal – courageously supported by peasant women and girls – successfully defended the gorge and the bridge against advancing superior Bavarian-French troops. With the construction of the legendary Arlbergbahn (1880–1884), the Imperial Royal Austrian State Railways acquired the castle, which had fallen into disrepair, as a material depot. Directly in front of the castle, the spectacular Trisannabrücke was erected in 1883/1884 – with a clear height of 87 metres and a span of 120 metres, the steel arch structure was considered at the time the second highest railway bridge in the world. At the end of the 19th century, the castle passed into private bourgeois hands and was restored in historicist style; it remains privately owned and permanently inhabited to this day.

Visit & Getting There

Burg Wiesberg is privately owned and not open to the public inside. However, the spectacular exterior views, the defensive walls, and the Trisannabrücke can be admired freely and completely free of charge year-round from viewpoints and hiking paths. Arrival by public transport: take ÖBB trains (Railjet or REX) to Bahnhof Landeck-Zams, then continue with VVT bus line 260 towards Ischgl/Galtür to the stop Pians Abzw. Tobadill or Pians Wiesberg. By car: via the S16 Arlbergschnellstraße expressway to the Pians/Paznaun exit, then follow the Silvretta Straße B188 uphill for about two kilometres; safe parking and photo laybys are located along the federal road directly below the castle rock near the Wiesberg-Kapelle.

Tips

The laybys along the Silvretta Straße and the forecourt of the Wiesberg-Kapelle are paved level and easily accessible by wheelchair or pram. An absolute photo tip for railway and architecture enthusiasts is the forecourt of the Neo-Gothic Wiesberg-Kapelle (built in 1884 upon completion of the viaduct): from here, the medieval castle walls and the crossing of modern ÖBB Railjet trains on the 87-metre-high Trisannabrücke unite into a picture-perfect panorama. Hikers can combine their visit with a tour along the Tiroler Burgenweg trail to Tobadill.
